report.title: 新手手冲：先润纸温壶
report.audience: 第一次在家做手冲咖啡、想快速理解润纸和温壶作用的新手。
objectives: 理解润湿滤纸可减少纸味并让滤纸贴合
知道润纸热水可顺便预热分享壶，减少温度流失
记住画圈润湿、倒掉水、再放粉的新手动作
了解豆子与水温仍会影响最终风味
report.arc: 从清晨台面的常见问题切入，先用动态对照解释润纸与温壶的两个作用，再把操作压缩成好记的三步动作，并补充风味变量边界。

chapters.title: 先别急着放粉
chapters.goal: 建立新手问题：干滤纸直接放粉为什么不稳妥。
chapters.narration: 手冲第一步，先别急着放粉。干滤纸直接冲，可能带纸味，还容易翘边；先润湿，会让滤纸贴紧滤杯。
chapters.reason: 用清晨厨房中的器具和直接对比开场，先回答用户指定的核心疑问，并为下一章温壶铺垫。

claims.text: 手冲教程建议在加入咖啡粉前用热水冲洗纸滤纸，否则纸滤纸可能带来纸味；热水同时会预热冲煮器具和杯壶。
画面把干滤纸可能翘边、水流不稳表现为示意，用于帮助新手理解，不宣称是实验测量结果。
claims.explanation: 来源明确支持冲洗滤纸可避免纸味并预热器具；脚本仅把贴合滤杯、水流更稳作为操作层面的直观示意，不编造定量流速。

visual.takeaway: 先润纸，滤纸更服帖，也少一点纸味。

items.label: 干滤纸直接冲
items.detail: 纸边翘起，可能带纸味；右侧用问号提示新手风险。

items.label: 热水润湿
items.detail: 细口壶沿滤纸内侧画小圈，纸边贴向滤杯壁。

items.label: 清晨台面
items.detail: 手冲壶、滤杯、滤纸和咖啡粉摆在暖光桌面。

chapters.title: 顺手温壶更稳
chapters.goal: 说明润纸的水落进分享壶可预热器具，帮助减少刚滴下时的热量流失。
chapters.narration: 润纸的热水流进壶里，顺手温一下分享壶再倒掉。咖啡滴下时，不被冷壶吸走热量，温度更稳。
chapters.reason: 把同一个小动作拆成润纸和温壶两个收益，避免新手以为只是多余步骤；温度影响由可靠冲煮资料支撑。

claims.text: Coffee Bros. 的手冲步骤说明，用热水冲洗纸滤纸的额外好处是预热冲煮器具和杯子或分享壶。
水温会影响咖啡萃取和风味平衡；手冲接触粉床和器具时会有热量损失，因此预热杯壶有助于减少刚开始滴滤时的温度波动。
claims.explanation: ref-4支持水温影响萃取、接触器具会产生温度损失；ref-2直接支持热水预热器具。脚本归纳为冷壶会吸走热量、温度更稳，不给出未经测量的具体降幅。

visual.takeaway: 同一股润纸水，先贴滤纸，再温分享壶。

items.label: 热水入壶
items.detail: 润纸后的热水沿滤杯落入分享壶，壶壁出现暖色升温示意。

items.label: 轻轻晃壶
items.detail: 分享壶轻轻转一圈，让热水接触壶壁，再把水倒掉。

items.label: 温度少波动
items.detail: 冷壶的蓝色寒意变淡，咖啡液滴入后保持暖色；为示意而非实测。

chapters.title: 记住三小步
chapters.goal: 给出好记动作并提醒豆子、水温等变量仍会影响风味。
chapters.narration: 记住三小步：画圈润湿，倒掉水，再放粉。这样冲更稳妥；不过豆子新鲜度、烘焙和水温，也会改变最后风味。
chapters.reason: 用简短口诀收束全片，并明确润纸温壶不是万能开关，风味还受用户要求提醒的豆子和水温影响。

claims.text: 给新手的操作口诀“画圈润湿、倒掉水、再放粉”依据手冲教程中先冲洗滤纸、预热器具、再加入咖啡粉的顺序整理。
claims.explanation: ref-2的步骤要求先冲洗纸滤纸并预热器具，之后才加入咖啡粉；脚本将其改写成易记的三个动作。

claims.text: 手冲咖啡的风味会受到咖啡豆品种、产地、烘焙等因素影响；研磨、比例、水温和时间也会改变冲煮结果。
新鲜整豆并在冲煮前研磨更有利于风味，咖啡豆新鲜度是新手需要关注的变量之一。

visual.takeaway: 画圈润湿，倒掉水，再放粉；豆子和水温也关键。

items.label: 1 画圈润湿
items.detail: 用少量热水沿滤纸内侧慢慢画一圈。

items.label: 2 倒掉水
items.detail: 把润纸兼温壶的热水倒出，不拿来冲咖啡。

items.label: 3 再放粉
items.detail: 滤纸服帖、分享壶温热后，再加入咖啡粉正式冲。

items.label: 风味还有变量
items.detail: 豆子新鲜度、烘焙度和水温都会影响杯中味道。

references.title: Pour-over coffee - NCA - About Coffee
references.excerpt: What is pour-over coffee? It’s pretty straightforward—you simply hand-pour water over coffee grounds in a filter, which extracts the flavors as it passes through the coffee grounds into a mug, carafe or container of your choosing. It’s a great option for coffee lovers who want to branch out and take more control over the brewing process. It’s a precise, manual process, so you get to learn a few new techniques , too! You can use any coffee beans you like, but what is pour-over coffee especially suited for? This method is known for bringing out distinctive flavors and aromas, so if you like single-origin coffees or other unique coffees, you should try using them for pour-over coffee. Sippable Fact Pour-over vs drip coffee—ever wondered what the difference is? Both methods involve pouring hot water through coffee grounds in a filter. However, while drip coffee is made by an automatic machine, you make pour-over coffee by hand-pouring the water, which usually takes more time than an automatic drip machine. While the methods are similar for pour-over vs drip coffee, they do have different advantages. Pour-over coffee can be more flavorful and is customizable, as you can fine-tune the entire brewing process to your taste. However, this method may only make one cup of coffee at a time, depending on the brewer, and it requires learning and using new techniques. Drip coffee is simple and convenient, and you can make a larger batch at one time with many drip coffee makers. But it doesn’t accentuate the flavors as much, and you have less control over the process overall. Here’s how to make pour-over coffee so that you get the best freshness and flavor—with tweaks that can help you find your perfect cup. Equipment To make pour-over coffee, you will need: Pour-over coffee brewer Filters Kettle or other hot water source Thermometer (unless one is built into kettle) Scale Grinder (optional, but preferred) Pour-over coffee brewers There are several different types of pour-over coffee brewers, or the device that holds the coffee filter and grounds. Filters are very important here! Pour-over coffee brewers are defined by the shape and function of their filters, which determine the pace of the brewing process. Ultimately, this can contribute to how your coffee will taste (along with other factors like the variety , origin , and roast of your coffee beans). Flat-bottom brewer This type of brewer has a flat bottom with three small holes, creating a slower and more even flow rate than other brewers and therefore making it easier to achieve a consistent brew. If you’re new to pour-over coffee brewing, this is a good brewer to try. Coffee cone/Conical brewer This brewer is cone shaped, with walls at a 60° angle, which creates a faster and more continuous flow rate. It requires some skill to pour evenly and ensure a consistent brew, making it a good choice if you’re more experienced with pour-over coffee and want to experiment. Coffee cone/Conical brewer designed with a carafe This brewer also has a cone shape, but it has a built-in carafe and a larger opening. However, it also uses a thicker filter, so the flow rate is slower than other conical brewers. It requires care and precision in pouring, so it’s probably a better fit if you’re more experienced—and especially if you want to brew larger batches of coffee. As you’re looking into pour-over coffee brewers, here are a few other key factors to keep in mind—and questions to ask yourself. Cost: What’s your price range for your brewer? Consider additional costs as well, such as any accessories you might want to buy, coffee filters that will need to be replenished, etc. Size: What will fit in the space you have? Capacity: How many cups of coffee do you need to make at one time? Design: Pour-over brewers are commonly sought after for their look and feel. What fits your aesthetic and the style of your kitchen? Customer reviews and ratings: There’s nothing like hearing from others who have used a coffee maker—what are they saying about your top choices? references.title: Perfect Pour Over Recipe: 6 Simple Steps – Coffee Bros.
references.excerpt: Pour Over Recipe With just an electric kettle, a dripper, and a filter, pour-over coffee brewing can produce a crisp, transparent, and refined cup of coffee. While this brewing technique can accommodate any coffee variety, we recommend using light to medium roasts with delicate acidity and a well-balanced taste. When appropriately executed, pour-over coffee brewing can offer some of the most outstanding coffee experiences. What You'll Need Brewing a pour-over at home can be as cheap as $75.00 to get started (this excludes a grinder) or as expensive as $375.00 (includes a high-quality grinder and electric kettle with temperature readings). Even if you opt for the lower end of the scale to get started where you buy pre-ground coffee ( not ideal you can read why here ), a Hario V60, and a pour-over gooseneck kettle you can be all in for less than $75.00. Even with this rookie starter pack, you will get more exceptional cups of coffee than when relying on an automatic drip machine. Equipment: Grinder or preground coffee (not ideal) Any pour-over device (We like the V60 or the Kalita Wave) Pour-over filter paper Gooseneck kettle Scale Important Factors Grind Size Medium coarse. You would adjust your grind size finer if your coffee brews too quickly and coarser if it brews too slowly. Brew Ratio 1 gram of coffee for every 14 grams of water for dark roasts and upward of 1 gram of coffee for every 17 grams of water for light roasts. Water Temperature Light Roasts : 203 - 212 degrees or right off boil Medium Roasts : 194 - 203 degrees Dark Roasts : 185 - 195 degrees Water Water represents 99% of the liquid in your cup so brewing with a good spring water makes all the difference. Coffee Always brew freshly roasted whole-bean coffee and grind on demand. The optimal timeframe to brew and enjoy your coffee is 7 – 30 days past the roast date. Measure Always time and measure your brews to understand better the outcome and one you can repeat our iterate on. 1 / of 6 Step 1: Measure and Grind Coffee Coffee amount: 15 grams Brew ratio: 1:15 (1 gram of coffee for every 15 grams of water) Your grind size and quality are crucial factors that will impact the length of your brew and the taste. For pour-over brewing, medium-coarse grind size is ideal for helping hit your target brew length of roughly 3:00 minutes. You will adjust your grind size finer if your brew length is too short and the cup comes out too sour. You will adjust your grinder coarser if your brew length is too long and the cup is too strong and bitter. Step 2: Rinse Your Filter Place your brewer and filter on top of your mug or carafe and rinse the paper filter with hot water; otherwise, it will give off a papery taste. The added benefit of using hot water here is that it warms up your brewing device and mug as you prepare the coffee for brewing. Step 3: Add Coffee and Heat Up Your Water Water Amount: 240 grams (8.5 ounces) First, add your coffee into the filter, place it on the scale, and tare it out. If your scale also has a timer, you will start the timer in step 4. Next, heat 240 grams of high-quality spring water to the ideal brewing temperature for the roast type (hotter for light roasts, cooler for darker roasts). Step 4: Bloom Bloom size: 45 grams (3- 4x coffee weight) Bloom length: 1:00 minute Your first pour is what is referred to as the “bloom.” The bloom allows your coffee to degas and helps with a more even extraction. If the coffee is fresh, you will notice the bed of grounds rises and bubbles during this step. For your bloom, we recommend 3 – 4x the weight of the coffee or 45 – 60 grams of water as your first pour. You want to ensure you saturate all the grounds in the bed of coffee, and you can even spin the brewer after the pour to help with the saturation. There are recipes recommending the bloom stage to last anywhere between 30 seconds and 2 minutes, and this is a great place to test what works best for the coffee you are brewing. Step 5: Remaining Pour Pour frequency: After the bloom is complete, pour the remaining water at 6-8 grams a second until you hit the final weight. references.title: Coffee: Brewing Temperature — SCA Standards and Extraction Effects — Coffee Tower
references.excerpt: Coffee: Brewing Temperature — SCA Standards and Extraction Effects Category: sensory-quality Updated: 2026-02-26 SCA brewing standard specifies 93°C ±2°C (200°F ±3°F); temperatures below 87°C produce under-extraction (sour, thin), while above 96°C over-extracts bitter compounds and degrades thermolabile acid structures. Key Data Points Measure Value Unit Notes SCA Brewing Target 93 °C (±2°C) 200°F ±3°F Under-Extraction Threshold 87 °C Below this: sour, thin, grassy flavors Over-Extraction Threshold 96 °C Above this: harsh bitterness dominates Cold Brew Temperature 4 °C 12–24 hour steep; very different extraction profile Espresso Brew Temperature 90–96 °C At puck; boiler typically set 6–10°C higher Water temperature is one of the most controllable variables in coffee brewing and has a direct, well-documented effect on extraction yield and flavor balance. The Specialty Coffee Association (SCA) specifies a brewing water temperature of 93°C ±2°C (200°F ±3°F), representing decades of empirical refinement. Why Temperature Matters Temperature governs the solubility and extraction rate of coffee’s chemical compounds. Coffee contains hundreds of soluble compounds, and they do not all dissolve at the same rate or respond to temperature identically: Acids (chlorogenic, citric, malic): Extract relatively quickly even at lower temperatures, and some thermolabile acids degrade at high temperatures. Sugars and Maillard compounds : Require adequate temperature to dissolve efficiently; contribute sweetness and body. Bitter phenolics and chlorogenic acid degradation products : Increasingly soluble at higher temperatures; extraction accelerates above ~93°C. Lipids and aromatic volatiles : Temperature-sensitive; higher temperatures can drive off desirable aromatics during brewing. Extraction Zones Temperature Range Extraction Character Dominant Flavors 4°C (cold brew) Extremely slow, 12–24h steep Low acidity, chocolate, mellow bitterness Below 87°C Under-extracted Sour, grassy, thin, sharp acidity, weak body 87–91°C Slightly under Bright, acidic, lighter body, acceptable 91–95°C (SCA target) Optimal extraction Balanced acid, sweetness, body, complexity 95–96°C Slightly over Increased bitterness, fuller body Above 96°C Over-extracted Harsh, astringent, bitter, flat 100°C (boiling) Severe over-extraction Rubbery, bitter, scorched notes Method-Specific Temperature Guidance Different brewing methods require slight adjustments within the SCA’s acceptable range: Pour-over (V60, Chemex, Kalita) : Many specialty baristas brew at 94–96°C to compensate for temperature loss during the pour. Each pour drops brew water temperature approximately 2–3°C as it contacts coffee grounds and the vessel. French press : A full-immersion method that retains heat better. 93°C is appropriate. Longer steep times (4 minutes) mean temperature drop is more significant — insulated vessels help. AeroPress : Versatile; lower temperatures (80–85°C) can produce interesting results with light roasts, exploiting selective acid extraction. Not under-extraction when intentional and balanced. Espresso : The boiler or heat exchanger is set higher than the actual brew temperature at the puck. A boiler set to 93°C might deliver water at 88–92°C at the group head, depending on machine design. E61 group heads thermally regulate but require careful flush protocols. Modern PID-controlled machines aim for 90–95°C at puck. Cold brew : Room temperature (20–22°C) or refrigerator temperature (4°C). 12–24 hour steeping time. The resulting concentrate has a distinct chemical profile — lower total acid, different bitter compound ratios, less aromatic complexity than hot brewed. Roast Level and Temperature Interaction Dark roasts have more porous, friable cell structure due to CO₂ degassing during roasting. They extract faster and at lower temperatures than light roasts. Brewing a dark roast at 96°C risks over-extraction and harsh bitterness. Light roasts, conversely, have denser cellular structure — slightly higher temperatures (94–96°C) help achieve adequate extraction. Roast Level Recommended Temperature Light / Nordic 94–96°C Medium 92–94°C Medium-Dark 91–93°C Dark 88–91°C Measuring Brew Tempe

references.title: Coffee Brewing | Hobby Portal
references.excerpt: Who It Suits Coffee brewing is the practice of extracting flavour from roasted, ground coffee with hot water. As a beginner you will spend most of your time at a kitchen counter: weighing coffee and water, grinding beans, pouring or pressing, and tasting the result. The main branches are immersion (French press, cold brew), pour-over and drip (cone brewers, filter machines), stovetop pressure (moka pot), and espresso — a high-pressure method that is a skill of its own and usually a later step. Coffee brewing suits people who enjoy small daily rituals, practical experimentation, and improving something they already drink. The honest appeal is that it is a cheap, repeatable craft: the same beans made with a slightly different grind or ratio taste noticeably different, so progress is something you can taste within a week. The honest constraints are that it needs a kettle, a little counter space, and care with hot water; that judging taste takes practice; and that the gear — grinders, scales, espresso machines — can quietly become expensive if you chase it. Getting Started Start with one simple method rather than buying a full coffee bar. A French press or a basic pour-over cone teaches the same fundamentals: ratio, grind, water temperature, and time. A reliable starting point, in line with the SCA’s brewing standards, is a brew ratio of about 1:15–1:18 (16–24 g of coffee per 100 g of water) with water just off the boil, roughly 90–96 °C (195–205 °F). For one cup that is about 15 g of coffee and 240–250 g of water. Buy whole beans roasted within the last few weeks if you can; ground coffee loses flavour within hours of grinding. Weigh coffee and water with a kitchen scale rather than scooping; it is the single biggest repeatability upgrade. Change one variable at a time (grind, ratio, temperature, time) so you know what made the cup better or worse. Keep short notes: beans, roast date, grind, ratio, time, and one taste word. You can learn entirely from your own notes, but local roasters often run free cuppings and brewing classes, and the SCA runs chapters and education courses in many countries — a fast way to get feedback on your cup. Key Terms Extraction — what brewing actually does: hot water dissolves soluble flavours out of ground coffee. Too little gives a weak, sour cup; too much gives a bitter, harsh one. Brew ratio — the proportion of coffee to water, written like 1:16 (one part coffee to sixteen parts water by weight). Grind size — how fine the beans are ground. Finer grinds extract faster and more; coarser grinds extract slower and less. It is the main dial for fixing a sour or bitter cup. Bloom — in pour-over, pouring a little water first to wet the grounds and let trapped CO₂ escape before the main pour. Under-extraction — a sour, thin, sometimes salty-tasting cup; usually fixed by grinding finer or brewing longer. Over-extraction — a bitter, dry, astringent cup; usually fixed by grinding coarser or brewing shorter. TDS (total dissolved solids) — how much is actually dissolved in the cup; a measure of strength. Roast date — when the beans were roasted. Freshness matters more than origin for most beginners. Single origin vs blend — beans from one region versus a mix designed for a consistent flavour. Arabica / robusta — the two main coffee species; most specialty coffee is arabica, while robusta is hardier, higher in caffeine, and common in espresso blends and instant coffee. Descaling — removing mineral buildup from kettles and machines with a mild acid (white vinegar or citric acid), done every few months depending on water hardness. Basic Gear Item Tier Typical price Buying criteria Kettle Must have $15–$60 Any kettle works to start. A gooseneck spout makes pour-over easier but is not required; a variable-temperature model is a later upgrade. One brewer Must have $10–$40 Pick one: French press, pour-over cone, moka pot, or a basic drip machine. Buy the cheapest decent version of the method you like. Kitchen scale Must have if buying one tool $10–$30 Choose a digital scale that reads to 1 g. It makes ratios repeatable and pays for itself quickly. request:
从零帮我生成一条30秒的新手冲咖啡小科普。就回答一个问题：手冲咖啡时为什么先把水倒在滤纸上润湿、顺便温一下分享壶，比干滤纸直接放粉冲更稳妥？用桌面手冲壶、滤纸、咖啡粉和清晨厨房的轻松画面说明，给一个好记的小动作，也提醒风味还会受到豆子和水温影响。
做成30秒竖屏视频，配音和字幕，画面用动态示意，给我可以播放的成片。

authorInput.narration: 做咖啡先别急着放粉。清晨台面备齐细口壶、滤杯、干滤纸和咖啡粉，先用热水润纸，少纸味。

visual.takeaway: 台面备齐器具，先润纸，少一点纸味。

items.label: 清晨厨房台面
items.detail: 暖光桌面依次出现细口手冲壶、滤杯、干滤纸和一碗咖啡粉。

items.label: 干滤纸直接冲
items.detail: 干滤纸旁标注“可能带纸味”，只提示新手风险，不表现实测流速。

items.label: 热水先润湿
items.detail: 细口壶向滤纸注入少量热水，纸味标识变淡；热水同时进入下方壶具。
